Topical cannabidiol is well tolerated
in individuals with a history of elite physical
performance and chronic lower extremity pain
Nicole Hall1,2, Bradie James3, Mohammad Alfrad Nobel Bhuiyan2,4, Erin Crane5, Carlie Falgout5 and
Kevin Sean Murnane1,2,5*   



  Abstract
  Introduction Cannabidiol (CBD) is a potential therapeutic for pain management. Yet, there exists a dearth of studies
  of its tolerability and efficacy, especially in special populations. Former elite athletes are a special population both sus-
  ceptible to chronic pain and also highly trained and attuned to assess medication tolerability concerns. The purpose
  of the present open-label pilot study was to assess the tolerability of CBD in this population.
  Materials and methods Retrospective analysis was conducted in deidentified data from 20 individuals who were all
  previously professional athletes in US/American football, track and field, or basketball, with careers ranging from 4 to
  10 years. Participants received topical CBD (10 mg twice daily by controlled dispenser) for chronic pain resulting from
  acute lower extremity injuries. Assessments of tolerability and secondary analyses of pain, pain-related disability, and
  activities of daily living were collected by self-report over the 6-week study period. Data were analyzed by descriptive
  statistics, pairwise t-test, and linear regression.
  Results Seventy percent of participants completed the study. Of the individuals who completed the study, 50%
  reported minor adverse effects, none of which required medical attention, and 50% did not report any adverse
  effects. The mostly commonly reported effects were skin dryness (43% of study completers) and skin rash (21% of
  study completers), which rapidly resolved. There was a significant improvement in self-reported pain levels (intake
  mean 3.5 ± 0.29; exit mean 1.7 ± 0.23; P < 0.001) and pain-related disability, including family and home responsibilities,
  life support activities, occupational activities, recreational activities, self-care, sexual function, and social activities (all
  P < 0.001).
  Discussion To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to assess CBD treatment in elite athletes, who are
  disproportionally susceptible to disabling injuries. Topical administration of CBD was tolerated well by this population
  and resulted in only minor adverse effects. As elite athletes are trained and attuned to assess their own bodies due
  to their professional lives, this population is likely to detect tolerability concerns. However, this study was limited to a
  convenience sample and self-reported data. These pilot findings warrant further study of topical CBD in randomized
  and controlled studies of elite athletes.
  Keywords Cannabidiol, Topical, Pain, Disability, Elite Athlete, Cannabinoid

 "evidenceSummary": "Two small laboratory studies of 10 people each. Study A (recreationally active men and women) compared a topical sodium bicarbonate lotion with oral bicarbonate in a cycling task to exhaustion; Study B (moderately trained male cyclists and triathletes) tested the lotion against placebo in three 30-second Wingate sprints. The lotion did not raise blood bicarbonate or pH, and it did not change time to exhaustion or sprint power in either study.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Two small repeated-measures lab studies of 10 people each, with no true placebo arm in Study A and no oral bicarbonate arm in Study B, so the lotion cannot be ranked directly against oral bicarbonate. The Study A oral condition also did not improve performance, which the authors attribute partly to variable responses in recreationally active participants.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read 'no improvement' as proof that topical bicarbonate does nothing in every sport, when the study tested one product at one matched dose in 20 people using short sprint and time-to-exhaustion tasks.",

  "citation": "McKay AKA, Peeling P, Binnie MJ, Goods PSR, Sim M, Cross R, et al. Topical Sodium Bicarbonate: No Improvement in Blood Buffering Capacity or Exercise Performance. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2020 (ahead of print).",
  "doi": "10.1123/ijspp.2019-0345",
  "abstract": "The study assessed a topical sodium bicarbonate lotion on blood buffering capacity and performance in recreationally active participants (study A) and moderately trained athletes (study B). In study A, the lotion did not raise pH or bicarbonate, while oral bicarbonate did, and cycling time to exhaustion did not differ (349 vs 363 s). In study B, the lotion did not change blood parameters, mean power or peak power. The authors conclude the lotion was ineffective in altering buffering capacity or enhancing performance.",
  "tldr": "A bicarbonate lotion applied to the legs did not raise blood buffering or improve sprint or time-to-exhaustion performance in these tests. Oral bicarbonate is the form with supporting evidence, and athletes should not switch to this lotion on the basis of this study.",
  "methods": "Study A: 10 recreationally active adults (7 men, 3 women) completed two counterbalanced double-blind trials of 30-second cycling efforts at 120% peak power to exhaustion, after either oral bicarbonate (0.3 g/kg) with placebo lotion or the lotion with an oral placebo. Blood was sampled over 90 minutes and after exercise. Study B: 10 moderately trained male cyclists and triathletes completed three 30-second Wingate sprints 30 minutes after either the lotion or a placebo lotion, in a randomized, double-blind design.",
  "findings": "In study A, oral bicarbonate raised blood bicarbonate and pH during recovery, while the lotion did not. Time to exhaustion was 363 s with oral bicarbonate and 349 s with the lotion (P = .697). In study B, mean and peak power did not differ between the lotion and placebo (P = .108 and P = .448).",
  "limitations": "Small samples, one product and one matched dose. The results and discussion report different bicarbonate rises for oral dosing at 90 minutes (4.7 vs 6.5 mmol/L), and the senior author accepted a scientific advisory board role with the product's company during peer review.",
  "practicalImplications": "Oral sodium bicarbonate (0.2 to 0.4 g/kg, 60 to 150 minutes before exercise) remains the form with evidence for performance gains of about 2 to 3% in efforts lasting 1 to 7 minutes, and the authors advise against substituting this lotion. Athletes using bicarbonate should individualize the protocol to limit GI distress and consult a sports nutrition professional.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Do not use this lotion as a substitute for oral bicarbonate for sprint or time-to-exhaustion performance. Any athlete considering a bicarbonate protocol should test oral dosing with a sports nutrition professional first, since this study did not support the lotion.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: Cannot inform return to sport. The participants were healthy adults and trained athletes, and the study did not assess injured or recovering athletes."
 }
}

              Topical Sodium Bicarbonate: No Improvement in Blood
                   Buffering Capacity or Exercise Performance
                           Alannah K.A. McKay, Peter Peeling, Martyn J. Binnie, Paul S.R. Goods,
                                       Marc Sim, Rebecca Cross, and Jason Siegler

     Purpose: To assess the efﬁcacy of a topical sodium bicarbonate (0.3 g/kg body weight NaHCO3) application (PR lotion; Amp
     Human) on blood buffering capacity and performance in recreationally active participants (study A) and moderately trained
     athletes (study B). Methods: In Study A, 10 participants completed 2 experimental trials: oral NaHCO3 (0.3 g/kg body weight +
     placebo lotion) or PR lotion (0.9036 g/kg body weight + oral placebo) applied 90 minutes prior to a cycling task to exhaustion
     (30-s sprints at 120% peak power output with 30-s rest). Capillary blood was collected and analyzed for pH, bicarbonate,
     and lactate every 10 minutes throughout the 90-minute loading period and postexercise at 5, 10, and 15 minutes. In Study B,
     10 cyclists/triathletes completed 2 experimental trials, applying either PR or placebo lotion 30 minutes prior to a cycling
     performance task (3 × 30-s maximal sprints with 90-s recovery). Capillary blood samples were collected at baseline, preexercise,
     and postexercise and analyzed as per study A. Results: In Study A, pH and bicarbonate were signiﬁcantly elevated from baseline
     after 10 minutes in the oral NaHCO3 condition and throughout recovery compared with no elevation in the PR lotion condition
     (P < .001). No differences in cycling time occurred between PR lotion (349 [119] s) and oral NaHCO3 (363 [80] s; P = .697).
     In Study B, no differences in blood parameters, mean power (P = .108), or peak power (P = .448) were observed between
     conditions. Conclusions: PR lotion was ineffective in altering blood buffering capacity or enhancing performance in either
     trained or untrained individuals.

 "evidenceSummary": "Cross-sectional study of 72 sports participants (45 men, 27 women) who trained at least twice a week in team or individual sports and had no Achilles tendon injury history. Each underwent MRI of both Achilles tendons, scored by a radiologist and by AI software, plus jump, balance, range-of-motion and muscle torque tests. In three of four functional groups, AI-based structural scores gave stronger correlations and more significant associations, and models explained 33 to 59% of functional variance with AI inputs versus 6 to 20% with radiologist inputs.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Cross-sectional and exploratory, with 72 people and many structure-function tests; models were built and scored on the same sample, so the variance figures are likely optimistic. The AI software belongs to the authors' company, which also funded the study, and the text says radiologist counts were higher for torque, which Table 3 does not show (12 AI vs 9 radiologist).",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the AI-based MRI scores as an injury screen for Achilles tendons, when the study links tendon structure to function in healthy athletes and does not test whether the scores predict injury.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,
  "citation": "Kapinski N, Jaskulski K, Witkowska J, Kozlowski A, Adamczyk P, Wysoczanski B, et al. Towards Achilles Tendon Injury Prevention in Athletes with Structural MRI Biomarkers: A Machine Learning Approach. Sports Medicine - Open. 2024;10:118.",
  "doi": "10.1186/s40798-024-00786-6",
  "abstract": "72 athletes had short-echo T2* gradient-echo MRI of both Achilles tendons, scored by a radiologist and by AI software, and were tested for dynamic strength, range of motion, muscle torque and balance. Structure-function correlations were modest (Spearman coefficients up to 0.49 for AI scoring), but structural features explained up to 59% of variance in functional groups with AI scoring, versus up to 20% with radiologist scoring. The authors conclude that AI-based scoring was superior and that the relationships are non-linear.",
  "tldr": "In healthy sports participants, Achilles MRI features relate to strength, balance and range of motion, and AI-based scoring linked structure to function more strongly than radiologist scoring. This is a cross-sectional association study, so it does not show that the scores predict Achilles injury.",
  "methods": "Cross-sectional study of 72 participants without Achilles injury history. Both tendons were scanned with a short-echo T2* gradient-echo sequence on 3T and 1.5T scanners and scored on six structural parameters by a radiologist and by SmarterOrthoMRI software. Functional tests were jumps on a force plate, single-leg balance, goniometer range of motion and muscle torque. Relationships were tested with Spearman correlation and normalised mutual information, and models (decision trees, random forests, AutoGluon) were trained with 10-fold cross-validation.",
  "findings": "AI-based structural scores gave higher maximal Spearman coefficients than radiologist scores in three of four functional groups (for example 0.49 vs 0.36 for range of motion). Table 3 counts more significant structure-function relationships with AI scoring in all four groups (for example 31 vs 29 for dynamic strength and 12 vs 9 for muscle torque), although the text says the torque count favored radiologists. Structural features explained 33 to 59% of functional variance with AI inputs and 6 to 20% with radiologist inputs.",
  "limitations": "A small cross-sectional sample with exploratory analyses; models were selected and scored on the same 72 participants, so explained variance is likely optimistic. The software belongs to the authors' company, which also funded the study, and the text's torque count conflicts with Table 3.",
  "practicalImplications": "Achilles MRI structure may help explain differences in strength, balance and mobility, and a short T2* protocol could be a candidate for screening studies. Do not use these scores to predict injury or make return-to-sport decisions until prospective studies support it.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: The findings link Achilles structure to strength, balance and range of motion in sports participants, which could guide future monitoring work. The study does not show that changing training according to the MRI scores improves performance or reduces injury.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: Limited. The participants were uninjured, so the study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions; prospective work in injured athletes would be needed before the scores are used for clearance."
 }
}

10	Towards Achilles Tendon Injury Prevention
11	in Athletes with Structural MRI Biomarkers: A
12	Machine Learning Approach
13	Norbert Kapinski1,2, Karol Jaskulski3, Justyna Witkowska2,4* , Adam Kozlowski2, Pawel Adamczyk2,5,
14	Bartosz Wysoczanski3, Agnieszka Zdrodowska3, Adam Niemaszyk3, Beata Ciszkowska-Lyson6 and Michal Starczewski3
15	
16	
17	  Abstract
18	  Background Recent advancements in artificial intelligence have proven their effectiveness in orthopaedic settings,
19	  especially in tasks like medical image analysis. This study compares human musculoskeletal radiologists to artificial
20	  intelligence in a novel, detailed, short, and cost-effective examination of Achilles tendon magnetic resonance
21	  images to uncover potential disparities in their reasoning approaches. Aiming to identify relationships between the
22	  structured assessment of the Achilles tendon and its function that could support injury prevention. We examined 72
23	  athletes to investigate the link between Achilles tendon structure, as visualised in magnetic resonance images using a
24	  precise T2*-weighted gradient echo sequence with very short echo times, and its functional attributes. The acquired
25	  data were analysed using advanced artificial intelligence techniques and reviewed by radiologists. Additionally, we
26	  conducted statistical assessments to explore relationships with functional studies in four meaningful groups: dynamic
27	  strength, range of motion, muscle torque and stabilography.
28	  Results The results show notable linear or non-linear relationships between functional indicators and structural
29	  alterations (maximal obtained Spearman correlation coefficients ranged from 0.3 to 0.36 for radiological assessment
30	  and from 0.33 to 0.49 for artificial intelligence assessment, while maximal normalised mutual information ranged from
31	  0.52 to 0.57 for radiological assessment and from 0.42 to 0.6 for artificial intelligence assessment). Moreover, when
32	  artificial intelligence-based magnetic resonance assessment was utilised as an input, the associations consistently
33	  proved more robust, or the count of significant relationships surpassed that derived from radiological assessment.
34	  Ultimately, utilising only structural parameters as inputs enabled us to explain up to 59% of the variance within
35	  specific functional groups.
36	  Conclusions This analysis revealed that structural parameters influence four key functional aspects related to the
37	  Achilles tendon. Furthermore, we found that relying solely on subjective radiologist opinions limited our ability to
38	  reason effectively, in contrast to the structured artificial intelligence assessment.
39	  Study Design Cross-sectional studies.

Towards Achilles Tendon Injury Prevention
in Athletes with Structural MRI Biomarkers: A
Machine Learning Approach
Norbert Kapinski1,2, Karol Jaskulski3, Justyna Witkowska2,4* , Adam Kozlowski2, Pawel Adamczyk2,5,
Bartosz Wysoczanski3, Agnieszka Zdrodowska3, Adam Niemaszyk3, Beata Ciszkowska-Lyson6 and Michal Starczewski3


  Abstract
  Background Recent advancements in artificial intelligence have proven their effectiveness in orthopaedic settings,
  especially in tasks like medical image analysis. This study compares human musculoskeletal radiologists to artificial
  intelligence in a novel, detailed, short, and cost-effective examination of Achilles tendon magnetic resonance
  images to uncover potential disparities in their reasoning approaches. Aiming to identify relationships between the
  structured assessment of the Achilles tendon and its function that could support injury prevention. We examined 72
  athletes to investigate the link between Achilles tendon structure, as visualised in magnetic resonance images using a
  precise T2*-weighted gradient echo sequence with very short echo times, and its functional attributes. The acquired
  data were analysed using advanced artificial intelligence techniques and reviewed by radiologists. Additionally, we
  conducted statistical assessments to explore relationships with functional studies in four meaningful groups: dynamic
  strength, range of motion, muscle torque and stabilography.
  Results The results show notable linear or non-linear relationships between functional indicators and structural
  alterations (maximal obtained Spearman correlation coefficients ranged from 0.3 to 0.36 for radiological assessment
  and from 0.33 to 0.49 for artificial intelligence assessment, while maximal normalised mutual information ranged from
  0.52 to 0.57 for radiological assessment and from 0.42 to 0.6 for artificial intelligence assessment). Moreover, when
  artificial intelligence-based magnetic resonance assessment was utilised as an input, the associations consistently
  proved more robust, or the count of significant relationships surpassed that derived from radiological assessment.
  Ultimately, utilising only structural parameters as inputs enabled us to explain up to 59% of the variance within
  specific functional groups.
  Conclusions This analysis revealed that structural parameters influence four key functional aspects related to the
  Achilles tendon. Furthermore, we found that relying solely on subjective radiologist opinions limited our ability to
  reason effectively, in contrast to the structured artificial intelligence assessment.
  Study Design Cross-sectional studies.

 "evidenceSummary": "PRISMA-guided scoping review of 79 English-language studies (2011 to July 2023) on GPS and local positioning systems in elite team sports, most in football and futsal. Studies were grouped by use: characterizing and comparing drills, training and matches (62%), correlational work (27%), injury or fatigue prediction (9%), and experimental work (3%), with nutrition covered by only two studies. Mean study quality was 89.2% on a 16-item appraisal, and few studies integrated external and internal load.",
 "screeningLimitations": "A scoping review with data extracted by one author and checked by another, moderate agreement on quality scoring (kappa 0.43), and exclusion of non-English work, prior systematic reviews and validity or reliability studies of tracking devices (n = 44). Its counts are descriptive and do not test the validity of any tracking metric.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read this as an endorsement of specific tracking metrics or a validated injury-prediction framework, when it maps how the research has been used, proposes an agenda, and excludes device validity studies.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2023,
  "citation": "Ferraz A, Duarte-Mendes P, Sarmento H, Valente-Dos-Santos J, Travassos B. Tracking devices and physical performance analysis in team sports: a comprehensive framework for research, trends and future directions. Frontiers in Sports and Active Living. 2023;5:1284086.",
  "doi": "10.3389/fspor.2023.1284086",
  "abstract": "This PRISMA-guided scoping review examined how GPS and local positioning tracking systems have been used in team-sport performance analysis from 2011 to 2023. Across 79 studies, tracking technology was used for match performance analysis, comparisons of training and match load, injury, and nutrition. Most work used kinematic and mechanical external-load metrics, with fewer studies integrating internal load. The authors propose a framework linking research strategies, metrics and applied decisions.",
  "tldr": "Tracking data are used mostly to describe match and training demands, with fewer studies predicting injury or fatigue and very few on nutrition. The authors call for a framework that links external and internal load, and for more experimental work.",
  "methods": "PRISMA-guided scoping review of PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus for English-language studies from January 2011 to July 2023 on GPS or local positioning systems with elite team-sport athletes. From 772 initial records, 79 studies were included after title and abstract screening and full-text review by two reviewers, with a third resolving disagreements. Quality was scored with a 16-item appraisal adapted from Faber et al. and Law et al.",
  "findings": "Studies came mainly from football (41.8%), futsal (15.2%) and rugby (11.4%). By analysis type, characterization and comparison of drills, training and matches was the largest group (62.0%), followed by correlational studies (26.6%), studies predicting performance, fatigue or injury (8.7%) and experimental studies (2.7%). Mean study quality was 89.2%.",
  "limitations": "Only English-language papers from three databases were included, and systematic reviews were excluded, so some relevant work may be missing. Reliability and validation studies were excluded, so the review does not judge device or metric validity, and quality scoring showed only moderate agreement (kappa 0.43).",
  "practicalImplications": "Teams should choose tracking metrics to fit the question and, where possible, track external and internal load together. The authors suggest chronic workload from tracking data is a better injury-risk indicator than total workload, but they note that no injury forecast yet links match-demand scenarios to load.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Use tracking data to compare training and match demands by position and session type, and check that the chosen metrics answer the coaching question. The review finds few studies on how training manipulations change match performance, so new drill designs should be trialled rather than assumed to work.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: Limited. The review covers healthy team-sport athletes and in-season injury studies; it does not evaluate rehabilitation or return-to-play criteria, so tracking data should not be used to clear players on this basis."
 }
}
